provisions.title: Aliens treated as applicants for admission

segments.t: An alien present in the United States who has not been admitted or who arrives in the United States (whether or not at a designated port of arrival and including an alien who is brought to the United States after having been interdicted in international or United States waters)
shall be deemed for purposes of this chapter an applicant for admission
All aliens (including alien crewmen) who are
applicants for admission or otherwise seeking admission
or readmission to or transit through the United States shall be inspected by immigration officers.

provisions.title: Arrest, detention, and release (excerpt)

segments.t: (a) On a warrant issued by the Attorney General, an alien may be arrested and detained pending a decision on whether the alien is to be removed from the United States.
Except as provided in subsection (c)

and pending such decision, the Attorney General
(1) may continue to detain the arrested alien; and
(2)
may release the alien on (A) bond of at least $1,500

with security approved by, and containing conditions prescribed by, the Attorney General; or (B) conditional parole . . . .

(c)(1) The Attorney General shall take into custody any alien who . . . (E)(i)
is inadmissible under paragraph (6)(A), (6)(C), or (7) of section 1182(a)

of this title; and (ii) is charged with, is arrested for, is convicted of, admits having committed, or admits committing acts which constitute the essential elements of any burglary, theft, larceny, shoplifting, or assault of a law enforcement officer offense . . . .

provisions.note: Subsection (c)(1)(E) was added by the Laken Riley Act in January 2025. Section 1182(a)(6)(A) covers people present without admission or parole.

segments.t: Any alien (other than an alien lawfully admitted for permanent residence) who . . . has been unlawfully present in the United States for one year or more, and who
again seeks admission
within 10 years of the date of such alien's departure or removal from the United States, is inadmissible.

topics.label: "Applicant for admission"
topics.question: Is "applicant for admission" a technical label that 1225(a)(1) attaches to everyone here without admission, or does it carry its everyday meaning of someone actually applying?

topics.label: "Seeking admission"
topics.question: Does "an alien seeking admission" describe someone presently trying to come in, or is it just another way of saying applicant for admission?

topics.label: Surplusage
topics.question: If the two phrases mean the same thing, did Congress write "seeking admission" into the provision for no reason, and does the canon against surplusage settle anything?

topics.label: The deeming clause
topics.question: When 1225(a)(1) says these individuals "shall be deemed" applicants for admission, does that legal fiction also make them people who are seeking admission?

topics.label: "Or otherwise seeking admission"
topics.question: Does the inspection provision's phrase "applicants for admission or otherwise seeking admission" show that applicants are a subset of those seeking admission, or that the two are different groups?

topics.label: "Again seeks admission"
topics.question: Does the word "again" in 1182(a)(9)(B), which applies to people who were unlawfully present, show that such people were already seeking admission?

topics.label: The inspection setting
topics.question: Do the references to an examining immigration officer and an applicant "clearly and beyond a doubt entitled to be admitted" show that the provision describes inspection at the border?

topics.label: Section 1226 and the Laken Riley Act
topics.question: Does the structure of 1226, including the 2025 Laken Riley Act amendment aimed at people who entered without inspection, show that Congress understood those people to be detained under 1226?

topics.label: Thirty years of practice
topics.question: How much weight belongs to nearly three decades in which five administrations held bond hearings for this group?

topics.label: Detention capacity
topics.question: Does Congress's failure to fund detention space for millions suggest it never mandated their detention?

topics.label: Scale of the change
topics.question: Would Congress make a change of this size through a cross reference, the "elephants in mouseholes" point?

topics.label: Avoidance and due process
topics.question: Should the statute be read to avoid serious constitutional questions about holding long time residents without any bond hearing?

topics.label: IIRIRA's purpose
topics.question: Did Congress in 1996 mean to end the "entry anomaly" that treated people who evaded inspection better than people who presented themselves at a port of entry?

topics.label: Supreme Court precedent
topics.question: What do Jennings v. Rodriguez, DHS v. Thuraissigiam, and related cases say about which statute governs?

annotations.summary: Treats "applicant for admission" as a statutory status covering people merely present without admission, unlike "applying for admission," which implies active steps, and on that basis rejects the government's (a)(4) argument and college applicant analogy.
annotations.quote: And that differs from the statutory meaning of "applicant for admission," which includes noncitizens taking no action at all who simply satisfy the passive condition of being present in the United States unlawfully.

annotations.summary: Holds that seeking admission means trying to gain lawful entry after inspection, so people who already entered unlawfully years ago are not seeking admission and fall outside 1225(b)(2)(A).
annotations.quote: Thus, the text leads us to the rather straightforward conclusion: Guerrero Orellana and his fellow class members are not "seeking admission" under § 1225(b)(2)(A) because they have already unlawfully entered the United States.

annotations.summary: Rejects the dissent's view that deeming someone an applicant also deems him to be seeking admission; the deeming text says nothing about seeking, and Sturgeon is distinguishable because there the statute stated the consequence.
annotations.quote: The problem is that this leap between the deeming language of § 1225(a)(1) and its alleged effect on § 1225(b)(2)(A) is contradicted by the text of § 1225(a)(1). The text "deem[s]" certain noncitizens "applicant[s] for admission" but says nothing to indicate that they are also deemed to be "seeking admission."

annotations.summary: Concedes or otherwise often signals a subset, but holds it can also mean something different, citing Helsinn and the advance parole example of applicants for admission who are not seeking admission.
annotations.quote: In this example, then, the government's argument that § 1225(a)(3)'s use of "or otherwise" indicates that "applicant for admission" is a smaller category necessarily included within the broader category of "seeking admission" fails.

annotations.summary: Holds the government's reading makes seeking admission superfluous, while the detainee's reading only limits applicant for admission; illustrates with travelers at a Dublin preinspection site who seek admission but are not applicants.
annotations.quote: The government, in interpreting "applicant for admission" and "seeking admission" as meaning essentially the same thing, reads "seeking admission," -- which, again, means seeking lawful entry -- out of the statute.

annotations.summary: Finds that 1226(c) mandatory detention for inadmissible noncitizens, especially the Laken Riley Act's subsection (E), would be duplicative under the government's reading, and rejects the parole limiting explanation as unsupported.
annotations.quote: If we accept the government's interpretation of § 1225(b)(2)(A) as already mandating the detention of all noncitizens present in the United States without admission, Congress's addition of subsection (E) through the Laken Riley Act was entirely duplicative.

annotations.summary: Reads the if clause as requiring an examining officer to decide whether someone may lawfully enter, a determination made at the time of entry at the border, not by ICE after an interior arrest.
annotations.quote: For § 1225(b)(2)(A) to apply then, the examining immigration officer necessarily must ascertain whether the noncitizen has a right to lawfully enter the United States.

annotations.summary: Adds, for anyone still doubtful, that five administrations over three decades applied 1226 to these detainees and Congress would not have tolerated a grossly mistaken reading of so large a detention mandate.
annotations.quote: Over three decades, five administrations implemented the disputed statutes just as we conclude today that their texts require.

annotations.summary: Contrasts IIRIRA's delayed implementation clause and modest bed increase for 1226(c) with silence on capacity for millions under 1225(b)(2)(A), concluding Congress scaled capacity only for the smaller criminal detention expansion.
annotations.quote: Instead of gearing up to newly detain millions of noncitizens present in the United States without inspection, IIRIRA's relatively modest uptick in detention capacity to "9,000 beds" by the end of fiscal year 1997 more logically reflects Congress's efforts to scale capacity

annotations.summary: Briefly invokes the elephants in mouseholes principle, reasoning that a massive detention increase with no provision for capacity is not something Congress would have enacted silently.
annotations.quote: In light of the massive increase in detention that the government's reading of § 1225(b)(2)(A) would require, IIRIRA's complete silence about how to address the resulting detention capacity gap tells the exact opposite story about congressional intent. After all, Congress "does not . . . hide elephants in mouseholes."

annotations.summary: Rejects the government's reliance on the House report entry doctrine passage, reading it as commentary on the 1101(a)(13) definition change that never mentions detention, so it does not show an intent to expand detention.
annotations.quote: Rather than being a general statement of congressional intent behind IIRIRA writ-large, this single-sentence excerpt from a 550-page report constitutes commentary about the amendment to a particular subsection of the INA, 8 U.S.C. § 1101(a)(13), which replaced the definition of "entry" with "admission" and "admitted,"

annotations.summary: Gives great weight to Jennings's description of 1225 as covering those seeking admission and 1226 those already present, relies on Preap, and reads Al Otro Lado and Lau as border cases supporting its view.
annotations.quote: In sum, Guerrero Orellana's interpretation of the disputed statutory provisions here aligns with Supreme Court precedent explaining how §§ 1225 and 1226 function.

annotations.summary: Argues 1225(a)(1) is not a definition of applicant for admission but a deeming provision, since Congress uses the word means when it defines terms, so the status carries legal consequences.
annotations.quote: If Congress wanted to define "applicant for admission," it could have done so by foregoing the term "deemed" and instead stating that an applicant for admission "means" an alien in the United States who has not been admitted or who arrives in the United States.

annotations.summary: Reads seeking admission as a reference back to applicant for admission rather than a separate condition, noting Congress did not use an is/and construction to require present affirmative conduct.
annotations.quote: Congress' choice not to do so suggests that "seeking admission" is not a standalone criterion requiring aliens to be making some present, affirmative action to seek admission.

annotations.summary: Treats 1225(a)(1) as a legal fiction that deems unadmitted people applicants seeking admission; says the majority's definitional exercise nullifies the deeming language and that Sturgeon does not require the consequence to be stated.
annotations.quote: This analysis is beside the point because § 1225(a)(1) expressly creates a legal fiction, deeming a person to be an applicant for admission who would not otherwise be considered an applicant seeking admission.

annotations.summary: Reads or otherwise in 1225(a)(3) as a catchall showing applicants for admission are a subset of those seeking admission, and distinguishes Helsinn as a reenactment case.
annotations.quote: This language strongly suggests that applicants for admission are deemed to be seeking admission. The word "otherwise" is a catch-all identifying that the items preceding it are subsumed by what comes after -- that is, it indicates a sub-set/super-set relationship.

annotations.summary: Finds support in 1182(a)(9)(B)(i)(I): the word again implies that prior unlawful presence itself counted as seeking admission, whether or not the person took affirmative steps.
annotations.quote: The use of the word "again" indicates that those who have been unlawfully present in the United States are deemed to have sought admission -- whether or not they took any affirmative action to do so.

annotations.summary: Accepts some redundancy as inartful drafting, since the canon is not an iron rule, and argues the detainee's reading creates the bigger surplusage problem by reading much of the deeming provision out of the statute.
annotations.quote: In any event, the surplusage canon raises a larger problem for Petitioner, given the intentional breadth of the deeming provision in § 1225(a)(1). A statute must generally be construed to give effect to every provision.

annotations.summary: Argues overlap is permissible: 1226(a) still governs admitted deportable people, 1226(c) adds deportable people and bars parole, and the Laken Riley Act had real effect while the Executive treated such people as bond eligible.
annotations.quote: My point, however, is a limited one: Regardless of Congress' intent, there is no reasonable dispute that the Laken Riley Act had the effect I have described; this is enough to give the amendments to § 1226(c) meaning.

annotations.summary: Disputes the majority's premise that inspection questioning happens only at the border, saying immigration officers can question unlawfully present aliens too and that the word may only makes the questions optional.
annotations.quote: But immigration officers can ask unlawfully present aliens these questions as well . . . and the use of the word "may" means only that the questions are not mandatory,

annotations.summary: Rejects the inference from IIRIRA's delayed implementation for 1226(c) but not 1225(b)(2)(A), offering plausible reasons Congress might not have expected a surge in noncriminal detention and calling such inferences speculation.
annotations.quote: The point is, we cannot divine Congress' expectations. Speculation as to Congress' choice is not a sound basis for reaching a conclusion contrary to the best reading of the statute.

annotations.summary: Argues Jennings and Preap do not make 1225 and 1226 mutually exclusive, calling the Jennings language background dicta, and notes another Jennings passage equates seeking entry with applicants for admission.
annotations.quote: So much is true; but, like Preap, Jennings does not compel the conclusion that § 1225(b)(2)(A) and § 1226 are mutually exclusive.

annotations.summary: Holds applicant for admission is a defined term with an artificial meaning covering constructive applicants who never applied, so the government's ordinary meaning comparison and college analogy do not work.
annotations.quote: Petitioner can therefore only be an "applicant for admission" because the statute uses "applicant" in a "specialized" way, rather than in its ordinary meaning.
cite: cert. granted sub nom. Rhoney v. Barbosa da Cunha

annotations.summary: Holds seeking, a present participle, means currently requesting lawful entry, so a person who entered twenty years ago and seeks only relief from removal is not seeking admission.
annotations.quote: Here, although Petitioner is an applicant for admission under the statutory definition because he is present in the country and has never been admitted, it simply cannot be said that he is "seeking admission," as he is not requesting lawful entry into the United States.
cite: cert. granted sub nom. Rhoney v. Barbosa da Cunha

annotations.summary: Says the word deemed confirms that applicant for admission is a legal fiction, but because Congress created no fiction for seeking, that phrase keeps its ordinary meaning and cannot be deemed.
annotations.quote: Thus, Congress here deemed, "abracadabra-style," . . . "applicant for admission" to cover noncitizens who literally cannot be applying for or seeking "admission." By contrast, the statute is silent on the meaning of "seeking" and "applying" and does not establish a legal fiction as to those terms, leaving them with their ordinary meanings.
cite: cert. granted sub nom. Rhoney v. Barbosa da Cunha

annotations.summary: Rejects the subset reading of or otherwise, citing Helsinn and Taylor, because 1225(a)(3) starts with the general term and follows with specific categories rather than a list of examples.
annotations.quote: By contrast, "applicant for admission" is not narrower or more specific than "alien seeking admission," nor does the statute enumerate multiple examples of "seeking admission."
cite: cert. granted sub nom. Rhoney v. Barbosa da Cunha

annotations.summary: Reads again seeks admission as covering those who previously sought lawful entry, noting the government's reading would erase differences among 1182(a)(9)'s distinct phrasings, and that again, if anything, implies one stopped seeking admission.
annotations.quote: If the government were correct that every "applicant for admission" has, by operation of law, sought admission, then there would be no need to specify "again," nor would there be any difference between "again seeks admission" and "seeks admission."
cite: cert. granted sub nom. Rhoney v. Barbosa da Cunha

annotations.summary: Holds the government's reading would render seeking admission mere surplus, while the detainee's reading gives both phrases a role by mandating detention only for those in both categories.
annotations.quote: Finally, if the government were right that "applicant for admission" is a subset of "seeking admission," there would have been no reason for Congress to use both.
cite: cert. granted sub nom. Rhoney v. Barbosa da Cunha

annotations.summary: Finds 1226(a) covers any alien pending removal, including inadmissible people, and that the government's reading would render much of 1226(c), including the 2025 Laken Riley Act amendment, superfluous.
annotations.quote: The government's interpretation also renders superfluous much of Section 1226(c), including amendments to that provision in the Laken Riley Act, which was passed by Congress in 2025.
cite: cert. granted sub nom. Rhoney v. Barbosa da Cunha

annotations.summary: Holds 1225(b)(2)(A) covers people presenting at a port of entry or caught at the threshold of entry, and notes the examining officer's present tense determination reinforces the current seeking requirement.
annotations.quote: Instead, Section 1225(b)(2)(A) applies to those noncitizens who present themselves at a port of entry for admission, or who cross the physical border into the United States but are apprehended at the "threshold of initial entry."
cite: cert. granted sub nom. Rhoney v. Barbosa da Cunha

annotations.summary: Treats nearly three decades of executive practice across five administrations, the 1997 regulation, and congressional silence through later amendments including the Laken Riley Act as strong evidence against the new reading.
annotations.quote: Even assuming arguendo that ambiguity existed in Section 1225(b)(2) with respect to its application to Petitioner and such ambiguity could support the government's position, the fact that the Executive Branch has for nearly three decades acted inconsistently with the newfound interpretation strongly counsels against adopting it.
cite: cert. granted sub nom. Rhoney v. Barbosa da Cunha

annotations.summary: Contrasts the safety valve Congress wrote for about 100,000 criminal detainees under 1226(c) with no capacity provision for an estimated two million people under the government's reading of 1225.
annotations.quote: The government offers no explanation for why the same Congress that was so concerned with the detention of 100,000 people under Section 1226(c) would have turned a blind eye to the consequences of mandating detention for all applicants for admission under Section 1225
cite: cert. granted sub nom. Rhoney v. Barbosa da Cunha

annotations.summary: Invokes extraordinary cases skepticism and elephants in mouseholes, reasoning that a seismic overhaul jailing millions would not be enacted through indirect, ambiguous text or a surreptitious again in 1182(a)(9).
annotations.quote: The government's interpretation of Section 1225(b)(2)(A) would send a seismic shock through our immigration detention system and society, straining our already overcrowded detention infrastructure, incarcerating millions, separating families, and disrupting communities.
cite: cert. granted sub nom. Rhoney v. Barbosa da Cunha

annotations.summary: Holds in the alternative that even if the text were ambiguous, constitutional avoidance would require rejecting the government's reading because categorical, potentially prolonged detention without bond raises serious due process problems.
annotations.quote: Finally, even if there were ambiguity in the statutory text, we would reject the government's interpretation because of the grave constitutional concerns it raises.
cite: cert. granted sub nom. Rhoney v. Barbosa da Cunha

annotations.summary: Rejects the government's reading of the House report as cherry picking; IIRIRA aimed at status and procedural inequities, not detention, and the government's reading itself treats illegal entrants worse than visa overstayers.
annotations.quote: As a result, the government erroneously concludes that IIRIRA sought to abolish all distinctions between arriving and already present noncitizens. It did not.
cite: cert. granted sub nom. Rhoney v. Barbosa da Cunha

annotations.summary: Gives great deference to Jennings's description of 1225 as operating at the border and 1226 for those already present, and limits Thuraissigiam's entry fiction to people caught at the threshold.
annotations.quote: The government points to no change in the legal landscape, and thus we afford great deference to the Court's description of the statutory scheme in Jennings.
cite: cert. granted sub nom. Rhoney v. Barbosa da Cunha

annotations.summary: Combines the statutory definition of admission with the meaning of entry as coming from outside to conclude seeking admission means trying to come in from abroad, which the petitioner is not doing.
annotations.quote: In short, someone who is "seeking admission" is trying to go from the exterior to the interior.
cite: cert. granted sub nom. Rhoney v. Barbosa da Cunha

annotations.summary: Agrees that treating every applicant for admission as seeking admission would make the latter phrase surplusage, and courts are loath to find Congress's words hollow.
annotations.quote: Third, Respondent's argument that all "applicants for admission" are necessarily "seeking admission" turns that latter phrase into surplusage.
cite: cert. granted sub nom. Rhoney v. Barbosa da Cunha

annotations.summary: Points to features of 1226, such as detention for state law offenses, roles for local authorities, and state attorney general standing, as showing its focus on the interior.
annotations.quote: Move along to § 1226, and its focus on the interior is likewise clear. It provides for the detention of certain aliens who violate state law
cite: cert. granted sub nom. Rhoney v. Barbosa da Cunha

annotations.summary: Stresses that admission requires entry after inspection, which settled case law places at a port of entry, and that 1225(b)(2)'s title refers to inspection at the border.
annotations.quote: And even if Petitioner were somehow seeking "entry," he surely is not seeking "entry . . . after inspection." Long-settled case law says that "inspection" ordinarily takes place at a port of entry
cite: cert. granted sub nom. Rhoney v. Barbosa da Cunha

annotations.summary: Notes five administrations from Clinton to Biden applied 1226 to interior detention, deserving substantial weight, and that a 1996 mandate for the largest mass detention in history would have been noticed sooner.
annotations.quote: If Respondent is right that in 1996 Congress ordered the largest mass detention in American history, the world would have likely noticed sooner.
cite: cert. granted sub nom. Rhoney v. Barbosa da Cunha

annotations.summary: Highlights that Congress gave a two year grace period and added beds for 1226(c) detention but no grace period for the two million people the government says 1225(b)(2) covered.
annotations.quote: Notably, Congress allowed no such grace period for the mandatory detention of the two million aliens that Respondent says then came within § 1225(b)(2)'s sweep.
cite: cert. granted sub nom. Rhoney v. Barbosa da Cunha

annotations.summary: Leads with Jennings, which describes 1225(b) as covering aliens seeking admission and 1226 as covering those already in the country, and says the passage is right even if dicta.
annotations.quote: Because Petitioner was "already in the country" and not "seeking admission into" it, his detention is governed by § 1226.
cite: cert. granted sub nom. Rhoney v. Barbosa da Cunha

annotations.summary: Holds 1225(a)(1) defines applicant for admission, calling the deemed versus defined distinction meaningless, and rejects the college analogy because the definition does not include seeking admission.
annotations.quote: This reasoning is inapt because Congress has given "applicant for admission" a specific definition that does not include the phrase "seeking admission."
cite: Buele Morocho v. Warden Phila. FDC

annotations.summary: Holds the present participle seeking requires present or ongoing affirmative action to gain lawful entry, and petitioners who entered years ago are taking no such action.
annotations.quote: By including this language, Congress specified what an "applicant for admission" must do to be subject to § 1225(b)(2)(A), namely engage in an ongoing affirmative act to "seek[] admission" to the United States.
cite: Buele Morocho v. Warden Phila. FDC

annotations.summary: Treats 1225(a)(1) as an ordinary statutory definition rather than a legal fiction, rejecting the government's reliance on the word deemed without engaging Sturgeon.
annotations.quote: We are not recognizing a legal fiction but rather are simply applying the statutory definition provided by Congress.
cite: Buele Morocho v. Warden Phila. FDC

annotations.summary: Rejects the subset reading of or otherwise because 1225(a)(3) does not list examples followed by a catchall; it simply makes both applicants and those seeking admission subject to inspection.
annotations.quote: Section 1225(a)(3) does not list several ways of "seeking admission," but rather merely states that "applicants for admission" and those "seeking admission" are subject to inspection—this use of "or otherwise" does not support the Government's position.
cite: Buele Morocho v. Warden Phila. FDC

annotations.summary: Holds that treating every applicant as seeking admission would make seeking admission surplusage, and that its reading gives every term meaning without departing from ordinary usage.
annotations.quote: If an "applicant for admission" were necessarily "seeking admission," then it would be unnecessary for § 1225(b)(2)(A) to specify that the noncitizen is "seeking admission."
cite: Buele Morocho v. Warden Phila. FDC

annotations.summary: Holds 1226(a) is not limited to admitted noncitizens and that the Laken Riley Act's 2025 addition to 1226(c) would be largely unnecessary if 1225(b)(2)(A) already covered unadmitted noncitizens inside the country.
annotations.quote: If one were to read § 1225(b)(2)(A) as mandating detention of unadmitted noncitizens within our borders, then § 1226(c) would be almost wholly unnecessary.
cite: Buele Morocho v. Warden Phila. FDC

annotations.summary: Reads 1225's title, its references to crewmen, stowaways, and contiguous territory, and the arriving alien regulation as showing the section governs inspection of people arriving at the border.
annotations.quote: Section 1225 is entitled "Inspection by immigration officers; expedited removal of inadmissible arriving aliens; referral for hearing," and accordingly uses terms focusing on individuals at the border.
cite: Buele Morocho v. Warden Phila. FDC

annotations.summary: Relies on the 1997 regulation and every later administration granting bond to those present without admission, plus Congress's failure to correct that practice, as evidence supporting its reading.
annotations.quote: In fact, when IIRIRA was passed, the Department of Justice explicitly recognized that noncitizens present in the United States were entitled to discretionary release . . . and every administration since has done the same
cite: Buele Morocho v. Warden Phila. FDC

annotations.summary: Notes Congress added only about 500 beds and paused implementation to handle criminal detention under 1226(c), making it doubtful IIRIRA silently mandated detention of millions more.
annotations.quote: Given the limited number of beds Congress mandated to accommodate the increased number of criminal noncitizens subject to removal without corresponding increases for noncriminal noncitizens, we are skeptical IIRIRA also mandated detention of, by Congress's count, millions of other noncitizens who had entered the country without admission.
cite: Buele Morocho v. Warden Phila. FDC

annotations.summary: Separately holds that detaining longtime residents without a bond hearing violates procedural due process under the Mathews balancing test, rejecting the government's reliance on Thuraissigiam.
annotations.quote: Thus, the Mathews factors weigh in Petitioners' favor, and their detentions without bond hearings violated their procedural due process rights.
cite: Buele Morocho v. Warden Phila. FDC

annotations.summary: Reads the House report as targeting procedural inequities between exclusion and deportation, not detention, and says Congress kept the bond distinction that favors interior entrants, so policy concerns cannot override the text.
annotations.quote: Although our holding affords bond to those who entered our borders without authorization while mandating detention for noncitizens who present themselves, Congress established this distinction in IIRIRA
cite: Buele Morocho v. Warden Phila. FDC

annotations.summary: Finds Jennings's dicta distinguishing 1225 and 1226 persuasive, and holds Thuraissigiam does not govern people who have lived in the country for decades with established connections.
annotations.quote: Their reliance on Thuraissigiam is misplaced as that case concerned the "entry fiction" doctrine as applied to a noncitizen apprehended within twenty-five yards of the border, i.e. "at the threshold of initial entry."
cite: Buele Morocho v. Warden Phila. FDC

annotations.summary: Argues 1225(a)(1) supplies a broad definition of applicant for admission for the whole chapter, so the term must carry the same full meaning in 1225(b)(2)(A), covering anyone present without admission.
annotations.quote: Section 1225(a)(1) supplies an explicit definition of "applicant for admission," and that definition governs wherever the defined term appears in the Chapter.
cite: Buele Morocho v. Warden Phila. FDC
, No. 26-1150, 2026 WL 2546223, at *16 (3d Cir. Aug. 28, 2026) (Mascott, J., dissenting).

annotations.summary: Argues seeking admission describes a status or state of being, not a discrete act, so anyone present without admission who desires to stay is seeking admission under ordinary meaning.
annotations.quote: Where an alien desires presence in the United States, he is "seeking" admission under the ordinary, common-sense meaning of the term.
cite: Buele Morocho v. Warden Phila. FDC
, No. 26-1150, 2026 WL 2546223, at *20 (3d Cir. Aug. 28, 2026) (Mascott, J., dissenting).

annotations.summary: Treats the deeming clause as assigning a legal status for the whole chapter without case by case inquiry, and says the majority's reading leaves it without the point Sturgeon requires.
annotations.quote: First, "deemed" is a legal command essentially creating a legal status of "applicant for admission" that applies to a broad class. Congress did not direct courts to ask, on a case-by-case basis, whether an alien colloquially has put forward an application for admission.
cite: Buele Morocho v. Warden Phila. FDC
, No. 26-1150, 2026 WL 2546223, at *16 (3d Cir. Aug. 28, 2026) (Mascott, J., dissenting).

annotations.summary: Reads or otherwise in 1225(a)(3) as a catchall making the seeking admission group broader than applicants for admission, not a narrower subcategory.
annotations.quote: It signifies the following phrase such as "seeking admission" is a catchall—making the reference broader, not narrower, than the group of "applicant[s] for admission."
cite: Buele Morocho v. Warden Phila. FDC
, No. 26-1150, 2026 WL 2546223, at *21 (3d Cir. Aug. 28, 2026) (Mascott, J., dissenting).

annotations.summary: Turns the canon around, arguing the majority's reading makes the reference to applicants for admission in 1225(b)(2)(A) meaningless, and that the final definite article the alien shows both phrases describe one group.
annotations.quote: They read the statute to require only a separate group, those actively "seeking admission," to be placed in mandatory detention. But then the § 1225(b)(2)(A) reference to the § 1225(a)(1) applicant class is meaningless and unnecessary.
cite: Buele Morocho v. Warden Phila. FDC
, No. 26-1150, 2026 WL 2546223, at *17 (3d Cir. Aug. 28, 2026) (Mascott, J., dissenting).

annotations.summary: Argues 1226(a)'s general reference to aliens yields to the more specific 1225(b)(2)(A) for unadmitted applicants, with 1226(a) mainly covering previously admitted people facing deportation; does not address the Laken Riley Act.
annotations.quote: But they misperceive the statutory scheme. Section 1226(a) references "alien[s]" in general, potentially extending to Petitioners here. But § 1225(b)(2)(A) is more specific—it mandates detention under § 1229a for all "applicant[s] for admission"
cite: Buele Morocho v. Warden Phila. FDC
, No. 26-1150, 2026 WL 2546223, at *13 (3d Cir. Aug. 28, 2026) (Mascott, J., dissenting).

annotations.summary: Argues the examining officer language assumes an officer for every applicant rather than limiting the provision to the border, and that exemptions for stowaways and contiguous land arrivals would be unnecessary under the majority's reading.
annotations.quote: But the reference to "examining immigration officer" assumes there will be such an officer anytime there is an applicant—§ 1225(b)(2)(A) refers to "the" officer, not "if an . . . officer determines."
cite: Buele Morocho v. Warden Phila. FDC
, No. 26-1150, 2026 WL 2546223, at *20 (3d Cir. Aug. 28, 2026) (Mascott, J., dissenting).

annotations.summary: Discounts decades of nonuse, comparing it to expedited removal and Title 42 authority that went largely unused for years before courts upheld their full use.
annotations.quote: Further, the § 1225(b)(1) expedited removal authority provides another clear, high-profile example of an Executive Branch policy determination not to use the full range of its removal or detention authority for decades after a statute's enactment.
cite: Buele Morocho v. Warden Phila. FDC
, No. 26-1150, 2026 WL 2546223, at *23 (3d Cir. Aug. 28, 2026) (Mascott, J., dissenting).

annotations.summary: Argues mandatory detention during removal proceedings is consistent with due process under Demore and related cases, that the hearing claim is really substantive, and that no history supports a right to bond.
annotations.quote: And Petitioners make no attempt to show a history or tradition of a constitutional right to release into the United States on bond during adjudication of an alien's claims to legal presence in the United States.
cite: Buele Morocho v. Warden Phila. FDC
, No. 26-1150, 2026 WL 2546223, at *27 (3d Cir. Aug. 28, 2026) (Mascott, J., dissenting).

annotations.summary: Argues IIRIRA eliminated the old regime favoring unlawful entrants, and the majority's reading recreates it by treating those who ask permission at the border more harshly than those who sneak in.
annotations.quote: It also would subject individuals who lawfully ask permission to enter the country to much tougher rules than people who submit formal requests to stay only once detained or inspected by immigration officials.
cite: Buele Morocho v. Warden Phila. FDC
, No. 26-1150, 2026 WL 2546223, at *10 (3d Cir. Aug. 28, 2026) (Mascott, J., dissenting).

annotations.summary: Relies on Thuraissigiam for treating illegal entrants as applicants for admission and avoiding a perverse incentive, and on Demore and related cases to uphold detention without bond hearings.
annotations.quote: under the statutory scheme even an "alien who tries to enter the country illegally" is nonetheless "treated as an 'applicant for admission.'"
cite: Buele Morocho v. Warden Phila. FDC
, No. 26-1150, 2026 WL 2546223, at *16 (3d Cir. Aug. 28, 2026) (Mascott, J., dissenting).

annotations.summary: Finds merit in both definitional and deeming readings of 1225(a)(1), suggests "applicant for admission" might best be understood as a term of art, and treats the statute as ambiguous on this point.
annotations.quote: Because Section 1225(a)(1) includes both people who are, by the ordinary meaning of the phrase, applicants for admission as well as those who must be designated as such for purposes of the law, the phrase "applicants for admission" might be best understood as a term of art.

annotations.summary: Holds "seeking admission" is an additional element describing active, ongoing conduct of applicants attempting lawful entry, typically at the border, which longtime residents like Petitioners are not engaged in.
annotations.quote: Seeking admission is a modifier indicating an additional element that must be met, not a characteristic imputed to every applicant for admission.

annotations.summary: Rejects the dissent's expansive reading of the deeming clause; even if 1225(a)(1) creates a legal fiction under Sturgeon, Hedin shows it deems people applicants only, not persons "seeking admission."
annotations.quote: Third, and significantly, even if Congress did intend to create a legal fiction by "deeming" the Petitioners to be "applicants for admission," it did not "deem" them to be "seeking admission," "applying for admission," or to have "submitted an application for admission."

annotations.summary: Rejects the government's "or otherwise" argument in a footnote, agreeing with the Second Circuit that the phrase does not always create a subset relationship and does not cure the ambiguity.
annotations.quote: As our colleagues at the Second Circuit have explained, however, "or otherwise" does not always create a subset relationship. . . . "Or otherwise" is context-dependent and does not cure the ambiguity of this statute.

annotations.summary: Applies the canons against surplusage and for meaningful variation: treating the phrases as synonyms writes "seeking admission" out of 1225(b)(2)(A), while Petitioners' reading gives every word effect.
annotations.quote: The Government's interpretation of Section 1225(b)(2)(A) collapses two distinct phrases, "applicant for admission" and "seeking admission," into one.

annotations.summary: Reads the 1226(c) carve outs, especially the Laken Riley Act's 1226(c)(1)(E), as proof that 1226(a) covers people who entered without inspection; the government's reading would give the 2025 amendment no effect.
annotations.quote: Under the Government's interpretation, these noncitizens would already have been subject to mandatory detention under Section 1225(b)(2)(A). The Laken Riley Act amendment would therefore have no effect.

annotations.summary: Traces the "clearly and beyond a doubt" language of 1225(b)(2)(A) to the 1893 border inspection statute and concludes "seeking admission" limits the provision to noncitizens at the border.
annotations.quote: Seeking admission is not surplusage. Rather, it is an essential phrase that limits the application of the subsection to noncitizens at the border.

annotations.summary: Treats three decades of uniform executive practice across five administrations, including the 1997 statement that people who entered without inspection are bond eligible, as weighty evidence for applying 1226(a).
annotations.quote: Since the passage of IIRIRA in 1996, 8 U.S.C. § 1226(a) has been universally understood to govern the detention of noncitizens, like Lopez Garcia and Rivera, who are already in the country, regardless of whether they entered the country lawfully.

annotations.summary: Contrasts Congress's worry that roughly 45,000 added 1226(c) detainees would strain detention resources, prompting delayed implementation, with its silence about detaining millions under the government's reading.
annotations.quote: Congress expressed concern that such an increase would place significant strain on existing detention resources and therefore provided for delayed implementation to allow time to scale up the nation's detention resources.

annotations.summary: Invokes the elephants in mouseholes canon: Congress would not have mandated detaining millions, an estimated six million today, through an ambiguous provision that no branch noticed for thirty years.
annotations.quote: As we have shown, the statute is riddled with ambiguity. We can safely assume that Congress would not have enacted such an historically unprecedented change without greater clarity.

annotations.summary: Applies constitutional avoidance, reasoning that mandatory detention without hearings for millions long present in the country would raise grave due process problems, while the bond hearing reading is fairly possible.
annotations.quote: This is a textbook case for constitutional avoidance. The Government's novel construction would implicate the constitutional due process rights of millions of noncitizens in our country, many of whom have lived, worked, and become integral parts of their communities, for years.

annotations.summary: Rejects the government's perverse incentive argument: IIRIRA equalized burdens and procedures in certain respects, but its text and history show no intent to erase every distinction or narrow bond eligibility.
annotations.quote: IIRIRA therefore made significant moves toward equalizing the treatment of noncitizens present in the country unlawfully and those who have just arrived. There is, however, nothing in the statutory text, structure, or history of IIRIRA to suggest that Congress intended, as the Government asserts, to eliminate every distinction between these groups.

annotations.summary: Relies on Jennings for the points that 1226(c) carves out of 1226(a) and that 1225(b)(2)(A) governs noncitizens seeking admission at the border; cites Thuraissigiam only on parole.
annotations.quote: By contrast, 8 U.S.C. § 1225(b)(2)(A), which does not allow for a bond hearing in advance of removal, has been understood to govern the detention of noncitizens "seeking admission into the country" at the border.

annotations.summary: Argues 1225(a)(1) is not a definition because it lacks "means" and sits outside 1101; "applicant for admission" keeps its ordinary dictionary meaning of one who requests lawful entry.
annotations.quote: Just as "vegetables" keeps its ordinary meaning, "applicant for admission" retains its definition as supplied by Section 1101(a)(13) and contemporary dictionaries.
cite: , No. 25-7044, 2026 WL 2661092, at *24 (4th Cir. Sept. 10, 2026) (Rushing, J., dissenting).

annotations.summary: Using dictionaries, reasons that an applicant is one who requests and seeking is requesting, so "applicant for admission" and "alien seeking admission" describe the same person.
annotations.quote: The result is straightforward: "applicant for admission" and "alien seeking admission" both refer to an alien who requests lawful entry into the United States. In other words, an applicant for admission is seeking admission.
cite: , No. 25-7044, 2026 WL 2661092, at *22 (4th Cir. Sept. 10, 2026) (Rushing, J., dissenting).

annotations.summary: Relying on Sturgeon v. Frost, treats 1225(a)(1) as a legal fiction with real effect: deeming Petitioners applicants places them in that posture, so they are deemed to be seeking admission.
annotations.quote: The statute deems aliens who actually are not applying for admission to be so. By deeming Petitioners to be persons who apply for admission, Section 1225(a)(1) deems them to be persons who seek admission.
cite: , No. 25-7044, 2026 WL 2661092, at *25 (4th Cir. Sept. 10, 2026) (Rushing, J., dissenting).

annotations.summary: Reads "or otherwise" in 1225(a)(3), consistent with other IIRIRA usages, to mean being an applicant for admission is one way of seeking admission, making applicants a subset of those seeking admission.
annotations.quote: The most natural reading of Section 1225(a)(3), then, indicates that being an "applicant[] for admission" is one "way or manner" of "seeking admission" and that aliens also can seek admission in "a different way or manner."
cite: , No. 25-7044, 2026 WL 2661092, at *27 (4th Cir. Sept. 10, 2026) (Rushing, J., dissenting).

annotations.summary: Concedes some redundancy but says the surplusage canon yields to ordinary meaning, and argues the majority's reading creates worse surplusage by leaving 1225(a)(1)'s coverage of present aliens no work in section 1225.
annotations.quote: As previously discussed, an applicant is one who seeks. Because the terms' ordinary meanings overlap, there is some redundancy between them.
cite: , No. 25-7044, 2026 WL 2661092, at *25 (4th Cir. Sept. 10, 2026) (Rushing, J., dissenting).

annotations.summary: Argues each 1226(c) subparagraph, including the Laken Riley Act's, reaches some people outside 1225(b)(2)(A) and removes parole eligibility, and that a 2025 Congress cannot fix the meaning of a 1996 statute.
annotations.quote: While this clause is another instance of overlap in subparagraph (E), it is not superfluous because it eliminates the possibility of parole that would otherwise be available to these individuals under Section 1182(d)(5)(A).
cite: , No. 25-7044, 2026 WL 2661092, at *30 (4th Cir. Sept. 10, 2026) (Rushing, J., dissenting).

annotations.summary: Rejects limiting 1225(b)(2)(A) to arriving aliens at the border: Congress said "arriving" elsewhere in section 1225 when it meant it, and 1225(b)(2)(C) covers aliens arriving between ports.
annotations.quote: Those provisions are strong evidence that Congress did not use the materially different phrase "alien seeking admission" when it meant "arriving alien."
cite: , No. 25-7044, 2026 WL 2661092, at *29 (4th Cir. Sept. 10, 2026) (Rushing, J., dissenting).

annotations.summary: Gives three decades of agency practice no weight: the 1997 bond policy was one conclusory sentence, a 1997 regulation applied 1225(b)(2), and unexercised authority does not evaporate.
annotations.quote: That the Executive long preferred the flexibility of Section 1226(a) over the rigidity of Section 1225(b)(2)(A) is unsurprising and is not evidence that the latter authority was never conferred.
cite: , No. 25-7044, 2026 WL 2661092, at *35 (4th Cir. Sept. 10, 2026) (Rushing, J., dissenting).

annotations.summary: Calls the detention capacity inference speculation that favors neither side, since the government never had capacity to detain everyone under section 1225, and Congress may have relied on parole or enforcement discretion.
annotations.quote: For one thing, it favors neither side because the Government "has never had sufficient detention capacity to maintain in custody every single person described in section 1225," under any interpretation.
cite: , No. 25-7044, 2026 WL 2661092, at *34 (4th Cir. Sept. 10, 2026) (Rushing, J., dissenting).

annotations.summary: Rejects the elephants in mouseholes objection: Congress spoke clearly by abandoning arrival based language and amending the detention provision itself, and section 1225 is no ancillary provision.
annotations.quote: But Congress did speak clearly in IIRIRA when it jettisoned all prior formulations of the detention provision that applied solely to arriving aliens and explicitly extended that provision to cover aliens present in the country who have not been admitted.
cite: , No. 25-7044, 2026 WL 2661092, at *33 (4th Cir. Sept. 10, 2026) (Rushing, J., dissenting).

annotations.summary: Rejects constitutional avoidance because detention pending removal, with parole available, raises no serious constitutional doubt under Demore, Flores, and Carlson, and removal safeguards are unaffected.
annotations.quote: The canon has no place here because the correct interpretation of the detention provision at Section 1225(b)(2)(A) does not "raise[] serious constitutional doubts."
cite: , No. 25-7044, 2026 WL 2661092, at *31 (4th Cir. Sept. 10, 2026) (Rushing, J., dissenting).

annotations.summary: Relies on Jennings's description of 1225(b)(2) as a catchall for all applicants not covered by 1225(b)(1), and on Demore to answer the due process concern.
annotations.quote: By contrast, the detention provision in Section 1225(b)(2)(A) draws no distinction between arriving aliens and those present in the United States. It covers any "alien who is an applicant for admission." . . . (Section 1225(b)(2) "serves as a catchall provision that applies to all applicants for admission not covered by § 1225(b)(1).")
cite: , No. 25-7044, 2026 WL 2661092, at *29 (4th Cir. Sept. 10, 2026) (Rushing, J., dissenting).

annotations.summary: Rejects Petitioners' term of art argument and reads "applicant" by its ordinary meaning, under which a person who applies for something is necessarily seeking it.
annotations.quote: Undeterred, the petitioners argue that "applicant for admission" is a term of art, so it cannot be understood according to its ordinary meaning. But the remaining provisions of § 1225 confirm that applicants for admission are indeed necessarily seeking admission.

annotations.summary: Using a college applicant analogy, rejects the present tense argument: no further affirmative act is needed, because an applicant keeps seeking admission while the application is pending.
annotations.quote: It would make no sense to say that as soon as the applicant clicks "submit" on her application, she is no longer seeking admission, merely because she does not take any further affirmative steps to gain admittance.

annotations.summary: Treats Petitioners as applicants for admission deemed by statute and reasons that while that status lasts through removal proceedings they are presently seeking admission; does not discuss Sturgeon or legal fictions.
annotations.quote: The petitioners are deemed, by statute, to be applicants for admission pending the resolution of removal proceedings. While they remain applicants, they are presently seeking admission.

annotations.summary: Reads "or otherwise" in 1225(a)(3), like "bike, jog, or otherwise exercise," to make applicants for admission a subset of those seeking admission; Petitioners' reading would make "otherwise" surplusage.
annotations.quote: The use of "or otherwise" suggests that "applicants for admission" are a subset of those "seeking admission."

annotations.summary: Says any redundancy does not license rewriting the statute, since redundancies are common and overlapping ordinary meanings make interchangeable use of the two phrases natural.
annotations.quote: That seems doubly true where the ordinary meaning of the terms involved overlap. Because being an applicant ordinarily entails seeking something, it seems natural to use the words somewhat interchangeably

annotations.summary: Holds 1226(c) still does work by reaching deportable aliens and barring parole, and the Laken Riley Act had real effect because the executive was then giving bond to the people it covers.
annotations.quote: Accordingly, the Act did have a substantial effect when passed insofar as it required the detention without bond or parole of certain aliens the administration was then treating as bond-eligible.

annotations.summary: Rejects reading "seeking admission" as "arriving alien," noting Congress used "arriving alien" elsewhere in section 1225, and says Petitioners' reading would eliminate inspection of unlawful entrants.
annotations.quote: To make matters worse for the petitioners, if Congress had intended an alien "seeking admission" to effectively mean "arriving alien," it would simply have said "arriving alien." Congress did not hesitate to use the "arriving alien" language elsewhere in § 1225.

annotations.summary: Holds 29 years of practice cannot override clear text, citing Pereira, and reads the 1997 Federal Register and a regulation as conceding that unadmitted aliens fell within section 1225.
annotations.quote: The text says what it says, regardless of the decisions of prior Administrations. Years of consistent practice cannot vindicate an interpretation that is inconsistent with a statute's plain text.

annotations.summary: Declines to draw meaning from Congress delaying 1226(c), but not 1225(b)(2)(A), over capacity concerns, saying the omission offers little insight into clear text.
annotations.quote: Congress could have declined to delay implementation of § 1225(b)(2)(A) for any number of reasons, and reading into a Congressional omission provides little insight, if any, into the meaning of clear text.

annotations.summary: In a footnote, rejects the dissent's mousehole charge because the text of 1225(b)(2)(A) is clear and 1225(a)(1) unambiguously has a sweeping scope.
annotations.quote: Because the text of § 1225(b)(2)(A) is clear, it is no mousehole, contrary to the dissent's characterization. Section 1225(a)(1) unambiguously has a sweeping scope

annotations.summary: Briefly dismisses fears of detention abuse as speculative and says Zadvydas has no direct application to aliens receiving due process during removal proceedings.
annotations.quote: In any event, Zadvydas v Davis . . . has no direct application to aliens who are detained and being given due process during removal proceedings.

annotations.summary: Says its reading better honors IIRIRA's goal of ending the entry anomaly, since preserving bond only for unlawful entrants would be strange, citing a 1997 Inspector General finding that most released aliens absconded.
annotations.quote: By eliminating the exclusion/deportation dichotomy, IIRIRA put aliens seeking admission lawfully on equal footing with those who entered without inspection. It seems strange to suggest that Congress would have preserved bond hearings exclusively for unlawful entrants.

annotations.summary: Treats Jennings's statement that 1225(b) covers aliens seeking admission as dicta, and reads Jennings's pairing of applicants for admission with aliens seeking entry as supporting the government.
annotations.quote: In determining that aliens lacked a statutory right to periodic bond hearings, the Jennings court did not opine on the difference between detention authority under § 1225 and § 1226. At most, the language petitioners cite is dicta.

annotations.summary: Treats "applicant for admission" as a defined statutory term of art and faults the majority for reading that definition back into the undefined phrase "seeking admission."
annotations.quote: "Applicant for admission," however, is a specifically defined statutory term of art in § 1225(a)(1); "seeking admission" is not. . . . The majority's attempt to read the definition of "applicant for admission" back into the phrase "seeking admission," as if sharing a word necessitates sharing a meaning, is unpersuasive.

annotations.summary: Reads "seeking" by its ordinary meaning and present participle form to require present, active conduct, actively seeking to enter, which Petitioners arrested inside the country were not doing.
annotations.quote: The ordinary meaning of "seek" requires some present, active action on the seeker's part.

annotations.summary: Answers the majority's question why 1225(a)(1) covers present noncitizens: the clause places them in the applicant category so they face the same removal proceedings, not mandatory detention.
annotations.quote: The answer is simple: § 1225(a)(1) does the crucial work of defining inadmissible noncitizens already in the country as within the category of "applicants for admission," which renders them subject to the same removal proceedings as noncitizens detained at ports of entry.

annotations.summary: Rejects the subset reading of "or otherwise," noting 1225(a)(3) mixes a noun with participial phrases and that "or otherwise" ordinarily refers to something different from what precedes it.
annotations.quote: There is thus no necessary subset-category relationship between "applicant for admission" and "seeking admission," even in § 1225(a)(3).

annotations.summary: Argues the government's reading leaves "an alien seeking admission" doing no independent work, violating the canon that every clause and word of a statute be given effect.
annotations.quote: On the government's reading, the phrase "alien seeking admission" does no independent work.

annotations.summary: Argues the Laken Riley Act and other 1226(c) exceptions for inadmissible noncitizens would be largely unnecessary under the government's reading, and rejects the parole elimination explanation.
annotations.quote: But this Act, and several of the other § 1226(c) exceptions referring to inadmissible noncitizens, would have been largely unnecessary if all inadmissible noncitizens were already subject to mandatory detention without a bond hearing under § 1225(b)(2)(A).

annotations.summary: Relies on section 1225's titles, its repeated references to arrival and inspection, and its descent from the 1893 border statute to read "seeking admission" as limiting it to arriving noncitizens.
annotations.quote: "[S]eeking admission" is therefore not a throwaway extra phrase, but rather the modern statute's equivalent of the key term limiting its reach to noncitizens "arriving" at the border.

annotations.summary: Treats nearly thirty years of unbroken practice under 1226, the 1997 Justice Department statement, and congressional acquiescence as independent reasons to reject the government's reading.
annotations.quote: the government's prior practice of detaining inadmissible noncitizens apprehended within this country under § 1226, not § 1225—unbroken for almost thirty years, not to mention the much longer historical practice from which it stems

annotations.summary: Contrasts Congress's provision to delay 1226(c), affecting about 45,000 people, over capacity concerns with the government's claim that IIRIRA silently required detaining millions.
annotations.quote: Congress specifically gave the Attorney General authority to defer the agency's much more modest implementation of § 1226(c)'s new detention mandate, which affected only persons subject to removal based on certain criminal offenses—an estimated 45,000 people in total—out of a recognition that this mandate alone would strain the agency's limited detention capacity.

annotations.summary: Calls the government's reading a quintessential elephant in a mousehole, citing major questions cases and the enormous impact of detaining potentially millions of long present noncitizens.
annotations.quote: This is a quintessential elephant-in-a-mousehole interpretation, and is all the more suspect because of the inconsistency of the agency's views and its longstanding failure to assert this hidden power.

annotations.summary: Answers the equalization argument: a single House Report sentence on 1225(a)(1) says nothing about detention, and Congress pursued equalization through other means such as unified removal proceedings.
annotations.quote: At its core, the government's argument hinges on some arguable statutory ambiguity at the margins and a single sentence of legislative history suggesting that the Congress that passed the IIRIRA wished to move toward equalizing the treatment of inadmissible noncitizens apprehended inside the country and those apprehended at the border

annotations.summary: Relies on Jennings's statement that 1225(b) covers aliens seeking admission and 1226 covers aliens already in the country, insisting lower courts are bound by such explications even if dicta.
annotations.quote: Second, Petitioners' reading of the text is confirmed by the Supreme Court's own clearly stated understanding of the difference between § 1225(b) and § 1226, and by the context and history of those provisions.

annotations.summary: Holds 1225(a)(1) defines "applicant for admission" as a term of art departing from ordinary meaning, so courts cannot break it apart and derive meaning from the word "applicant."
annotations.quote: Section 1225(a)(1) sufficiently indicates Congress's intent for the phrase "applicant for admission" to bear a meaning different from any ordinary meaning.

annotations.summary: Relying on dictionaries and the present participle, holds "seeking admission" requires actively pursuing lawful entry through inspection, which Petitioners, who avoided inspection, were not doing.
annotations.quote: These definitions, in addition to Congress's definition of "admission," demonstrate that for a noncitizen to be "seeking admission" under § 1225(b)(2)(A), the noncitizen must actively be in search of lawful entry into the United States via inspection and authorization by an immigration officer.

annotations.summary: Rejects the dissent's view that 1225(a)(1) merely lists who is treated as an applicant, calling it a distinction without a difference because presence alone departs from ordinary meaning.
annotations.quote: After all, § 1225(a)(1)'s designation that mere presence in the United States makes for an "applicant for admission" departs from the ordinary meaning of "applicant." . . . The phrase itself thus evades ordinary understanding.

annotations.summary: Rejects the subset reading of "or otherwise," finding no list for ejusdem generis and noting stowaways and some permanent residents seek admission without being applicants.
annotations.quote: But it is not the only way. The word "otherwise" can refine the subsection's scope as opposed to indicating relation between the two phrases.

annotations.summary: Rejects the dissent's Lemus-Losa argument, holding "again" limits 1182(a)(9)(B)(i)(II) to those who previously sought admission and now seek it again, not to mere unlawful presence.
annotations.quote: The word "again" in the provision has force. It limits the category of noncitizens who are deemed inadmissible in this provision to those who have sought admission or lawful entry in the past and are again seeking admission.

annotations.summary: Applies the surplusage canon: if "seeking admission" lacked independent meaning, Congress could have written only "applicant for admission," and the dissent's withdrawal theory does not cure the problem.
annotations.quote: If "seeking admission" did not have independent meaning, then Congress could have simply written § 1225(b)(2)(A) without the phrase and instead employed "applicant for admission." To hold otherwise would render § 1225(b)(2)(A)'s use of "seeking admission" superfluous.

annotations.summary: Notes 1225(b)(2)(A) applies only after an examining immigration officer's determination, while interior relief claims go to immigration judges; it expressly declines to address border only arguments.
annotations.quote: But for noncitizens like Petitioners who are within the interior, these claims for relief are typically presented before and resolved by an immigration judge, who is expressly not an immigration officer.

annotations.summary: Treats the government's unbroken 29 year practice of applying 1226(a), including the 1997 interim rule allowing bond hearings, as consequential evidence under Loper Bright.
annotations.quote: Finally, the government's previously unbroken 29-year streak of applying § 1226(a) as opposed to § 1225(b)(2)(A) to noncitizens like Petitioners is consequential.

annotations.summary: Contrasts IIRIRA's capacity escape hatch for about 45,000 added 1226(c) detainees with the absence of any provision for the millions who would be detained under the government's reading.
annotations.quote: This is all to say that Congress was well aware of the gargantuanly large population of "applicants for admission" when it passed IIRIRA but expressed no concern as to the logistical nightmare implicated by the government's interpretation of § 1225(b)(2)(A)'s mandatory detention scheme.

annotations.summary: Separately holds that detaining long term residents without an individualized bond hearing violated due process, rejecting the government's reliance on Thuraissigiam and Demore.
annotations.quote: We find no error in the district courts' conclusions that Petitioners were due individualized bond hearings in light of the significant time they have spent within the interior of the United States.

annotations.summary: Acknowledges IIRIRA aimed to remedy the entry anomaly but says it did so through other changes, and appeals to that purpose cannot override the text.
annotations.quote: IIRIRA thus has already done much to address this anomaly. But appealing to this congressional purpose can only go so far.

annotations.summary: Relies on Jennings's description of 1225(b) for those seeking admission and 1226 for those already present, and confines Thuraissigiam to the border and Demore to 1226(c).
annotations.quote: Put differently, § 1225(b)(2)'s mandatory detention scheme applies to certain noncitizens who seek admission into the country, whereas § 1226's permissive detention scheme applies to all other noncitizens pending a decision on their removability, with exceptions.

annotations.summary: Argues 1225(a)(1) is not a definition, since it says "deemed" and sits outside 1101, so the undefined word "applicant" takes its ordinary meaning of one who applies for or seeks.
annotations.quote: Because the paragraph nowhere defines the word "applicant," it is inevitable that courts must give some definition to this word. And I would use its ordinary meaning when applying the law.

annotations.summary: Reads the participle to require seeking in progress at inspection, but says deemed applicants remain applicants while present, a constructive pending application, so they continue to seek admission.
annotations.quote: And the ongoing status of being an applicant implies that the person continues to seek the applied-for item (unless the applicant seeks to withdraw the application).

annotations.summary: Treats the deeming clause as a legal fiction requiring courts to regard present noncitizens as applying for or seeking admission wherever the INA uses those phrases.
annotations.quote: In other words, by "deem[ing]" certain immigrants to be "applicant[s] for admission" under the INA . . . the law commands us to treat them as if they were applying for (or seeking) admission wherever the INA uses those phrases

annotations.summary: Reads "otherwise" to mean in a different way, so 1225(a)(3) shows being an applicant for admission is one way of seeking admission, and rejects four competing explanations.
annotations.quote: So the paragraph conveys that being an "applicant for admission" is one of several ways of "seeking admission."

annotations.summary: Adopts the BIA's Lemus-Losa reasoning that "again seeks admission" in 1182(a)(9)(B)(i)(II) assumes prior unlawful presence already counted as seeking admission, supporting his reading.
annotations.quote: As the Board of Immigration Appeals has explained, the word "again" in this provision would serve no purpose unless the prior unlawful presence itself qualified as the first time that the immigrant was "seeking admission."

annotations.summary: Answers the surplusage objection by saying "seeking admission" excludes applicants who withdraw and depart under 1225(a)(4), and that redundancy is common in immigration statutes anyway.
annotations.quote: Congress might have used the phrase "seeking admission" to exclude "applicants for admission" who seek to withdraw their applications and depart the country at the time of their inspection.

annotations.summary: Argues 1226(c) and the Laken Riley Act are not superfluous because they impose arrest duties and narrower release rules, and may have clarified a practice that gave bond to criminal immigrants.
annotations.quote: In sum, the INA prioritizes the arrest, detention, and removal of criminal immigrants under any interpretation of § 1225(b)(2)(A). So the Laken Riley Act also is "not superfluous" under my reading.

annotations.summary: Rejects limiting 1225(b)(2)(A) to arriving immigrants: Congress used "arriving" elsewhere in section 1225 and dropped "port of arrival" and "entry," so a subtle participle cannot impose that limit.
annotations.quote: If Congress had meant to restrict mandatory detention to the narrow range of immigrants who are both on the border and claiming to be admissible, one would have expected to see it in a clear standalone requirement—not a subtle participle clause.

annotations.summary: Gives prior practice no weight because long practice cannot override text, citing Pereira, and the 1997 bond position was one unreasoned sentence that conflicted with the agency's parole view.
annotations.quote: But the Petitioners identify no reasoned opinion from the Executive Branch that supports their view. To the contrary, the government adopted that view in one conclusory sentence soon after IIRIRA's enactment

annotations.summary: Rejects the detention capacity inference as speculation, suggesting Congress may have expected parole or enforcement discretion to relieve capacity concerns under 1225(b)(2)(A).
annotations.quote: Or perhaps Congress thought the "parole option" under § 1182(d)(5)(A) would relieve any detention-capacity concerns with § 1225(b)(2)(A).

annotations.summary: Rejects avoidance because the text is unambiguous and finds no due process problem under Demore, Flores, and Carlson, since detention pending removal is permissible and parole remains available.
annotations.quote: In these circumstances, the Petitioners' temporary detention during their "removal proceedings" represents a "constitutionally permissible part of that process."

annotations.summary: Relies on IIRIRA's elimination of the entry anomaly and says Petitioners' reading would expand the perverse incentive to enter unlawfully; also cites that incentive as a rational basis for detention.
annotations.quote: The Petitioners' view thus would read IIRIRA to expand (rather than eliminate) the "perverse incentive to enter at an unlawful rather than a lawful location" that existed before Congress passed that law.

annotations.summary: Says Jennings decided a different question and should not be parsed like a statute, adding that its catchall description of 1225(b)(2) favors the government; relies on Thuraissigiam and Demore on due process.
annotations.quote: Because Jennings did not consider the scope of § 1225(b)(2)(A), I would not overread any language about the specific contours of the respective sections.

annotations.summary: Treats 'applicant for admission' as a term of art defined by 1225(a)(1), so Congress's artificial meaning displaces ordinary meaning and cannot import the ordinary sense of seeking.
annotations.quote: Section 1225(a)(1) explains "applicant for admission" as a term of art—relevant here, as "[a]n alien present in the United States who has not been admitted." This artificial "deeming" mandates that the ordinary meaning of "applicant for admission" must give way to Congress's chosen definition.

annotations.summary: Holds that undefined 'seeking admission' takes its ordinary meaning of affirmative pursuit, and Cirrus Rojas, who entered unlawfully years ago and seeks only asylum and similar relief, is not seeking admission.
annotations.quote: To read Section 1225(b)(2)(A)'s use of "seeking admission" as merely another way of saying "applicant for admission" ignores that while "applicants for admission" may literally "seek admission," they do not always do so.

annotations.summary: Reads the deeming clause as a legal fiction that makes him an applicant but, citing Sturgeon, does not conjure a fictional intent to seek admission; mixing fiction with fact is error.
annotations.quote: While Section 1225(a)(1)'s "deeming" language may make Cirrus Rojas an applicant for admission "abracadabra-style," . . . it does not conjure a fictional intent to seek admission. Congress holds the magic wand to "deem" that statutory terms carry a specific meaning in this context; the Executive does not.

annotations.summary: Rejects the government's subset reading of 'or otherwise' in 1225(a)(3), noting the phrase can also denote something different, and finds a disjunctive reading fits the INA better.
annotations.quote: But "or otherwise" can also "refer to something that is different from something already mentioned." . . . And as we discuss below, a disjunctive reading of Section 1225(a)(3)—treating "applicant for admission" and "seeking admission" as distinct—better fits within Section 1225 and the INA as a whole.

annotations.summary: Finds the government's reading writes 'seeking admission' out of 1225(b)(2)(A), while its own reading gives both phrases independent work, and rejects the government's claim of surplusage within 1225.
annotations.quote: These examples show that "applicant for admission" and "seeking admission" are distinct—both do independent work in Section 1225 and the INA overall. Some "applicants for admission" are also "seeking admission," and some are not.

annotations.summary: Says treating 1226(c) as redundant violates the surplusage canon, because the 2025 Laken Riley Act expansion would have been unnecessary if 1225(b)(2)(A) already mandated detention of all inadmissible aliens present here.
annotations.quote: There was "no need" for Congress to amend Section 1226(c) in this way if Section 1225(b)(2)(A) "had always covered" all inadmissible aliens present in the United States and required detention without bond.

annotations.summary: Reads 'the examining immigration officer' as evoking a specific border examination, notes it is unclear who examined an interior arrestee, and says 1225(a)(4) and (a)(5) make sense only at the border.
annotations.quote: This language suggests contact at the border, not the interior: DHS's own regulations outline a border-specific "examination" process applying to individuals presenting "in person to an immigration officer at a U.S. port-of-entry when the port is open for inspection."

annotations.summary: Treats nearly thirty years of practice by five administrations, and Congress's failure to correct it even when passing the Laken Riley Act, as confirming that 1225(b)(2)(A) applies only at the border.
annotations.quote: Until last year, all three branches of our government agreed that Section 1225(b)(2)(A) applied only at the border. Five successive presidential administrations followed this interpretation. And the Executive's sudden about-face presents its own reason to doubt the government's new reading.

annotations.summary: Finds it telling that Congress delayed 1226(c) for lack of detention space but made no similar provision or funding for 1225(b)(2)(A), which would have covered at least two million people.
annotations.quote: That Congress did not enact a similar provision for Section 1225(b)(2)(A)—which would have mandated detention for at least two million people in 1996—is telling.

annotations.summary: Invokes the elephants in mouseholes principle, rejecting the idea that Congress tucked the broadest mass detention mandate in the nation's history into an obscure clause and never funded it.
annotations.quote: Put simply, Congress does not hide "elephants in mouseholes." . . . The government asks us to accept that Congress in 1996 tucked "the broadest mass-detention-without-bond mandate in our Nation's history" into an obscure corner of its new law and has never bothered to fund it for three decades since.

annotations.summary: As an alternative ground, says the government's reading raises grave due process concerns by allowing detention without purpose or risk findings, supporting avoidance, though these concerns do not drive the holding.
annotations.quote: And at minimum, there is a very real risk that the government's reading will sweep in others like Cirrus Rojas who have already been found not to be dangers or flight risks. The Due Process Clause forbids such arbitrary detention. This alone makes us doubt the government's interpretation as a matter of constitutional avoidance.

annotations.summary: Says legislative purpose cannot displace text and that IIRIRA's equalizing aim targeted disparities in removal procedures between lawful and unlawful entrants, not detention pending removal.
annotations.quote: Whatever IIRIRA's various "purposes" may have been, they were far more nuanced than what the government asserts. Its amendments to the INA show that Congress focused on eliminating disparities between lawful and unlawful entrants in removal procedures, not pre-removal detention.

annotations.summary: Treats Jennings's border versus interior description as nonbinding dicta but another data point for its reading, and in a footnote limits Thuraissigiam to people in that petitioner's position near the border.
annotations.quote: But at minimum, the Supreme Court's unquestioning recitation of the border-interior distinction between Sections 1225 and 1226 is another data point suggesting that Cirrus Rojas's reading is correct.

annotations.summary: Reads 1225(a)(1) as a statutory classification making all unadmitted aliens, arriving or present, applicants for admission subject to the same inspection, removal, and detention procedures.
annotations.quote: Section 1225(a)(1) deems both arriving and unlawfully present aliens as "applicants for admission." And by design, all applicants for admission are subject to the same inspection and removal procedures.

annotations.summary: Concludes that nothing in the statute, including the use of the verb 'seeking' instead of the noun 'applicant', shows Congress meant to treat present aliens differently from arriving ones.
annotations.quote: In my view, they are also subject to the same mandatory-detention requirement. Nothing in the statute—and certainly not the use of the verb "seeking" in lieu of the noun "applicant"—suggests that Congress intended otherwise.

annotations.summary: Views the deeming clause as creating a constructive application by operation of law, so Cirrus Rojas must be treated as seeking admission whether or not he actually is.
annotations.quote: By operation of law, he is an "applicant for admission" and must be treated as if he is applying for or seeking admission into the United States regardless of whether he is in fact doing so.

annotations.summary: Describes 1225(a)(3) as the inspection mandate but says debates over the meaning of 'otherwise', like dictionary definitions, cannot resolve the case.
