annotations.quote: analogies to real-world uses of the word "admission," and the various meanings of the word "otherwise" do not—cannot—resolve this case.

annotations.summary: Argues 1182(a)(9)(B)(i)'s 'again seeks admission' makes sense only if seeking admission includes being treated as an applicant because of unlawful entry, undercutting the majority's literal reading.
annotations.quote: If "seeking admission" means in fact "seeking admission," then the presence of "again" makes no sense. If, by contrast, that phrase means "being treated as an applicant for admission by virtue of an unlawful entry," then the use of "again" is perfectly coherent.

annotations.summary: Considers the surplusage canon inconclusive, observing that every canon has exceptions and that incongruities arise under both sides' readings of the INA.
annotations.quote: For every grammatical thrust, there is a parry; for every canon of construction, there is an exception that calls for the canon to give way.

annotations.summary: Concedes 1225's inspection questions fit oddly for a longtime resident, but says the provision's application is fixed by law rather than by the facts of an individual case.
annotations.quote: It would indeed be odd to ask Cirrus Rojas, who has been living in the United States for eight years and who was arrested without warning, whether he "intends to remain permanently" in the country.

annotations.summary: Explains that IIRIRA cured the anomaly favoring those who evaded inspection by making admission the touchstone, putting all unadmitted aliens on equal footing as applicants for admission.
annotations.quote: By reorienting removal procedures around an alien's admission by immigration authorities rather than his physical entry into the country, Congress eliminated the procedural windfall that had long accrued to aliens who evaded inspection at the border.

annotations.summary: Cites Jennings's description of 1225(b)(2)(A) as a catchall for all applicants for admission, arguing the majority shrinks it to a subset of arriving aliens.
annotations.quote: And it relegates § 1225(b)(2)(A)'s detention mandate from "a catchall provision that applies to all applicants for admission not covered by § 1225(b)(1)," . . . to a far more limited provision that applies to only a subset of arriving aliens

annotations.summary: Rejects Avila's term of art argument, reasoning that even if 'applicant for admission' is a term of art, the text shows it means the same thing as 'seeking admission'.
annotations.quote: Avila also asserts that "applicant for admission" is a term of art with special meaning, but this argument is similarly unavailing. Because the text does not indicate that "seeking admission" and "applicant for admission" are different, they still mean the same thing even if "applicant for admission" is a term of art.

annotations.summary: Agrees with the Fifth Circuit that applying and seeking share an ordinary meaning, and holds that 1225(b)(2)(A)'s structure does not make seeking admission a separate condition for detention.
annotations.quote: Here, we agree with the Fifth Circuit that the ordinary meanings of the phrases "applicant for admission" and "seeking admission" are the same.

annotations.summary: Reasons that just as a present alien is an applicant without filing an application, he is likewise seeking admission without literally asking, so seeking mirrors the term of art meaning.
annotations.quote: In other words, just as an alien is an "applicant for admission" even though no literal "application" is filed, so too is an alien "seeking admission" even when the alien does not literally "request" or "ask for" admission into the country.

annotations.summary: In a footnote, says 1225(a)(3)'s 'or otherwise seeking admission' shows any distinction between the phrases is irrelevant, endorsing the Fifth Circuit's view that applicants are a subset of those seeking.
annotations.quote: the statutory context constrains and limits any distinction to a level of irrelevance. This is made evident in the plain language of 8 U.S.C. § 1225(a)(3), which says that "[a]ll aliens . . . who are applicants for admission or otherwise seeking admission . . . shall be inspected by immigration officers."

annotations.summary: Rejects the surplusage objection, reasoning that Congress may use synonyms and that the statute's structure gives 'seeking admission' no standalone meaning, so redundancy is not decisive.
annotations.quote: Since the structure of the text does not indicate that this phrase has standalone meaning, merely using it as a synonym for something else does not make it surplusage.

annotations.summary: Says 1226(c), including the Laken Riley Act, reaches deportable aliens and bars parole, so overlap with 1225(b)(2)(A) is not surplusage and may reflect Congress being doubly sure.
annotations.quote: Because § 1225(b)(2)(A) broadly applies to any alien who is "seeking admission," and because, as established earlier, the text is clear that this phrase is synonymous with "applicant for admission," any overlap between § 1225(b)(2)(A) and the Laken Riley Act is just that—overlap.

annotations.summary: Answers the border limitation argument by noting 1225(a)(1) distinguishes aliens who have not been admitted from those who arrive, so the statute reaches the interior as well as the border.
annotations.quote: In distinguishing an alien "who has not been admitted" from one "who arrives," the text makes clear that it applies to aliens in the nation's interior as well as at the border.

annotations.summary: Holds that prior administrations' limited use of 1225 cannot narrow the statute, because authority granted by Congress does not evaporate through lack of administrative exercise.
annotations.quote: Thus, even if previous administrations did not exercise their full authority under § 1225, the "[a]uthority granted by Congress . . . cannot evaporate through lack of administrative exercise,"

annotations.summary: Rejects the argument that Congress's failure to delay 1225(b)(2)(A) for detention capacity, as it did for 1226(c), shows a narrower reading, calling it speculation drawn from legislative history.
annotations.quote: However, Avila's argument is unconvincing because "it is never our job to rewrite . . . statutory text under the banner of speculation about what Congress might have done."

annotations.summary: Relies on IIRIRA's goal of placing all unadmitted aliens on equal footing, finding it incongruous that unlawful entrants would get bond hearings while those engaging the legal process would not.
annotations.quote: Because this outcome is incongruous and contradicts the statute's goal of placing all aliens "on equal footing," it cuts against Avila's reading of the statute.

annotations.summary: Treats Jennings's border and interior description as nonbinding background dicta that does not preclude applying 1225 to aliens arrested in the interior.
annotations.quote: But this characterization was offered only as general background information, as the Court there was not confronted with the interpretive issue now before us.

annotations.summary: Faults the majority for using the statutory definition to deem Avila an applicant and then the ordinary meaning of the same phrase to find him seeking admission.
annotations.quote: To get to its desired result, the court uses the statutory definition to deem Avila an "applicant for admission," and then turns around and uses the ordinary meaning of the same phrase to find he is also "seeking admission" when he is not.

annotations.summary: Reads 'seeking' as a present participle expressing present action, so 1225(b)(2)(A) covers only aliens presently trying to gain lawful entry after inspection, which Avila was not doing.
annotations.quote: Applying the ordinary meaning of the word "seeking" and the statutory definition of "admission," § 1225(b)(2)(A) applies to aliens presently trying to gain lawful entry into the United States after inspection and authorization by an immigration officer.

annotations.summary: Argues the majority renders 'seeking admission' superfluous, while Avila's reading gives effect to every word by requiring both applicant status and actual seeking.
annotations.quote: While the court's interpretation renders "seeking admission" superfluous, Avila's interpretation gives effect to every word in § 1225(b)(2)(A) by applying only when an alien is both (1) an "applicant for admission" and (2) actually seeking admission.

annotations.summary: Argues the 1226(c) exceptions for inadmissible aliens, including the Laken Riley Act provision for those who entered without inspection, would be superfluous, showing Congress understood 1226(a) to cover them.
annotations.quote: When Congress enacted the Laken Riley Act, it acted with the understanding that § 1226(a) applied to at least some inadmissible noncitizens.

annotations.summary: Points to 1225's title referring to inspection by immigration officers and arriving aliens, and to the phrase 'seeking admission', as preserving the border detention distinction.
annotations.quote: The IIRIRA maintained this distinction as evidenced by Congress's use of "seeking admission" and § 1225's title, which continues to refer to "Inspection by immigration officers" and "expedited removal of inadmissible arriving aliens."

annotations.summary: Stresses that five administrations and most immigration judges applied 1225 only at the border, and that Congress never corrected that view, which courts should consider.
annotations.quote: Five presidential administrations, including the first Trump administration, and most immigration judges interpreted § 1225 to apply only to those arriving at the border. This conduct is something courts ought to consider.

annotations.summary: Notes Congress deferred 1226(c) for two years to build detention capacity but made no such provision for 1225(b)(2), consistent with the traditional reading.
annotations.quote: This comported with Congress's decision when it passed the IIRIRA to authorize deferred implementation of § 1226(c) for two years while the agency increased its detention capacity, . . . while making no such provision for implementation of § 1225(b)(2).

annotations.summary: Says IIRIRA fixed the entry anomaly for removal proceedings but kept the bond distinction for detention, and rejects the majority's perverse incentive rationale.
annotations.quote: Despite the well-established understanding and application of § 1225(b)(2), the court reaches a different result, pointing to the perverse incentive it creates.

annotations.summary: Relies on Zadvydas for the principle that the distinction between those who have entered and those who have not runs throughout immigration law.
annotations.quote: But as the Supreme Court has recognized, "[t]he distinction between an alien who has effected an entry into the United States and one who has never entered runs throughout immigration law"

annotations.summary: Following Torres, treats 'applicant for admission' as a term of art conferring a fictive legal status on people outside its plain meaning, so it cannot be equated with 'seeking admission' by ordinary meaning.
annotations.quote: For all these reasons, we conclude that "applicant for admission" in § 1225 is best treated as a term of art used to identify a class of people that do not meet the plain meaning understanding of that term, and that imbues them with "a fictive legal status."

annotations.summary: Reads the present participle 'seeking' as describing active effort to gain entry, and holds that a person living in the interior is not in a perpetual state of seeking entry.
annotations.quote: In ordinary usage, however, we would not normally regard someone present in the United States to be in the perpetual state of "seeking" entry into the United States.

annotations.summary: Says placing people in an unordinary legal classification through deeming does not mean they take on other statutory attributes sharing that term's ordinary meaning, as its college analogy shows.
annotations.quote: When people are placed into a legal classification that—as a matter of ordinary meaning—would not typically apply to them ("applicants for admission"), it does not mechanically follow that those people should thereby fall within other aspects of the statute that otherwise would share an ordinary meaning with what is in fact an unordinary term-of-art classification.

annotations.summary: Finds 'or otherwise' in 1225(a)(3) ambiguous, noting the subset reading would also make applicants a subset of those seeking readmission or transit, so the provision is at best a wash.
annotations.quote: But in that scenario, "applicants for admission" would also be a subset of those seeking "readmission to or transit through the United States," . . . which does not easily follow. In short, § 1225(a)(3) is at best a wash for the question before us.

annotations.summary: Holds the government's reading leaves 'seeking admission' without independent meaning, and because the phrase is integral to triggering examination and detention, the usual tolerance for surplusage is weaker here.
annotations.quote: For one, if all applicants for admission are necessarily "seeking admission," as the government maintains, it is unclear why Congress would have included the phrase "seeking admission" in § 1225(b)(2)(A).

annotations.summary: Reasons that 1226(c), including the Laken Riley Act's 1226(c)(1)(E), shows 1226(a) covers inadmissible aliens present without admission, and that the government's reading makes the recent amendment largely irrelevant.
annotations.quote: In any event, for present purposes the point is that in considering the statutory scheme as a whole, § 1226(c)(1)(E) more strongly supports the conclusion that the aliens it covers who did not commit qualifying criminal acts are already covered by § 1226(a).

annotations.summary: Reads 'examining immigration officer' as describing a formal examination traditionally conducted at the border, noting predecessor statutes used the same phrase and tied it explicitly to the port of arrival.
annotations.quote: This is corroborated by the fact that, in the pre-IIRIRA statutory predecessors for mandatory detention, Congress similarly used the phrase "examining immigration officer" and explicitly tied application of the provision to the border.

annotations.summary: Treats thirty years of consistent executive practice granting bond, the government's Jennings briefing, and congressional silence across many amendments as strong evidence the claimed detention mandate does not exist.
annotations.quote: The dissent therefore errs in suggesting that all we have here is Executive Branch "inactions." . . . We have thirty years of action—the government actively treating unadmitted aliens present in the interior of the country as entitled to bond hearings under § 1226(a).

annotations.summary: Notes Congress delayed 1226(c) to build detention capacity, showing capacity was a countervailing concern that may explain why Congress did not mandate detention of some two million interior aliens.
annotations.quote: But we need not theorize as to why Congress did not delay implementation of § 1225(b)(2)(A) to make the more basic observation that the delay afforded for § 1226(c) shows that detention capacity is a countervailing concern when it comes to how many aliens Congress may wish to place in mandatory detention.

annotations.summary: Says Congress would not make a sharp break toward mass detention through a cross referenced deeming provision, citing Whitman and MCI, and expects clearer language for such a fundamental change.
annotations.quote: We may fairly ask: if the statute is meant to require the mass detention of unadmitted aliens present in the United States and mark a sharp break from the past, would Congress have introduced such a major change through a cross-referenced deeming provision, in the way the government asserts?

annotations.summary: Accepts IIRIRA sought equal footing in removal but says that need not extend to detention, that expedited removal addresses entry incentives, and that perverse incentive concerns cannot override text.
annotations.quote: Thus, to the extent there is concern that the traditional understanding of § 1225(b)(2)(A) lowers the costs of illegal entry, the expedited removal and other detention provisions, as well as the criminal prohibitions, address this concern to some degree.

annotations.summary: Relies on Jennings's descriptions of 1225 as applying to aliens seeking entry and 1226 to those already present as reflecting the traditional understanding of the two provisions.
annotations.quote: This language in Jennings indicates that the Supreme Court was evidently operating on the same understanding of §§ 1225 and 1226 that has prevailed since 1996 (and earlier, under the predecessor provisions)

annotations.summary: Applies an ordinary, nonspecialized meaning to 'applicant for admission', rejecting the majority's term of art treatment drawn from Torres, which he says addressed a different provision.
annotations.quote: Second, I apply a non-specialized, ordinary meaning to both the phrases "applicant for admission" and "seeking admission" as neither phrase is defined in the statute.

annotations.summary: Concludes an applicant for admission is one who applies, and applying for admission is synonymous with seeking admission; the verb form does not change the meaning.
annotations.quote: As several judges before me have noted, an applicant for admission is one who applies for admission, and the ordinary meaning of "apply for admission" is synonymous with "seeking admission." The use of the gerund does not change its meaning.

annotations.summary: Citing Sturgeon, argues the deeming clause must carry consequences, so deemed applicants take on the plain meaning traits of applicants, including seeking admission; otherwise the clause becomes a nullity.
annotations.quote: It strains belief that Congress would go to the trouble of "deeming" a group of aliens "applicants for admission" if it did not intend for that group of aliens to assume any of the characteristics of the plain meaning of those words.

annotations.summary: Reads 'or otherwise' in 1225(a)(3) as showing applicants for admission are a subset of those seeking admission, calling this the simplest and most natural reading.
annotations.quote: That the words "or otherwise" set off "applicants for admission" from "seeking admission" demonstrates that Congress denoted applicants for admission as a "subset" of those seeking admission.

annotations.summary: Says the surplusage canon is not decisive because redundancy is common, the plaintiffs' reading creates its own redundancy, and 'seeking admission' may exclude those withdrawing under 1225(a)(4).
annotations.quote: In these circumstances, when both sides' interpretations could introduce some surplusage, we cannot prioritize a desire to avoid redundancy over the plain text of the statute Congress enacted.

annotations.summary: Says 1226(a) and 1226(c) still do independent work for admitted aliens and parole, and the Laken Riley Act overlap carries little weight given longstanding nonenforcement when it passed.
annotations.quote: And as to the Laken Riley Act amendments under § 1226(c)(1)(E) in particular, any presumption against surplusage is substantially weakened by the fact that Congress passed that Act in 2025, against the backdrop of longstanding nonenforcement of § 1225(b)(2)(A) to the class of aliens relevant to this case.

annotations.summary: Rejects limiting 'examining immigration officer' to border inspectors, reasoning that an ICE agent fits the statutory definition and necessarily finds an alien who entered without inspection inadmissible.
annotations.quote: The majority seeks artificially to limit the definition of an "examining immigration officer" to someone behind a numbered window, counter or desk, with papers before him, to the exclusion of the ICE agent on the dusty road in Texas or the street corner in the Los Angeles barrio.

annotations.summary: Dismisses decades of executive nonenforcement as an exercise of discretion that cannot change the text, and cites 1997 regulations as showing the agency recognized its detention power.
annotations.quote: That the executive branch had until this point exercised its discretion in deciding not to detain aliens present without admission under § 1225(b)(2)(A) is irrelevant. Such previous governmental practice does nothing to change the text of the statute.

annotations.summary: Rejects inferences from Congress's delay of 1226(c) for detention capacity as speculation, suggesting Congress may have had other reasons not to delay 1225(b)(2)(A).
annotations.quote: This argument invites undue speculation as to what Congress would have done and why it would have done so. Although the plaintiffs would have us infer from the delay in implementation Congress's understanding of the statutory text, the delay could also reflect Congress's understanding of the executive's then-intended enforcement agenda.

annotations.summary: Doubts the major questions doctrine applies, citing immigration's foreign affairs dimension and that detention is within the agency's wheelhouse, and says no heightened clarity requirement is appropriate.
annotations.quote: While the majority is correct that the Supreme Court has employed this heightened standard in recent Major Questions Doctrine cases, many of which the majority cites, as Judge Lagoa made clear, it is doubtful that the doctrine applies to the case at hand.

annotations.summary: Relies on IIRIRA's purpose, recognized in Torres, of ending the anomaly favoring unlawful entrants, arguing the majority's reading would restore the perverse incentive to enter unlawfully.
annotations.quote: The majority's interpretation would thus reintroduce the very inequality that Torres told us Congress sought to remedy in IIRIRA: that our immigration laws would incongruously privilege those who enter this country illegally and evade detection, as compared to those who responsibly present themselves at ports of entry consistent with legal requirements.

annotations.summary: Does not engage Jennings's own border and interior description; in a footnote, discounts the government's Jennings briefing as reciting past practice rather than conceding what 1225 and 1226 mean.
annotations.quote: This recitation of past usage was not a comment on the meaning of the text of §§ 1225 and 1226 and was certainly not a concession that § 1225(b)(2)(A) could not be used to detain aliens present within the country.

annotations.summary: Treats "applicant for admission" as a defined term under 1225(a)(1) and faults the government for using its statutory meaning to cover the petitioner but its ordinary meaning to equate it with seeking admission.
annotations.quote: Like Schrödinger's cat is simultaneously dead and alive, "applicant for admission" simultaneously takes on both its ordinary and statutory meanings in the Government's hands.

annotations.summary: Reads the present participle "seeking" to require present, ongoing action requesting lawful entry, which a person who already entered and lives in the interior cannot take, so 1225(b)(2)(A) is limited to the border.
annotations.quote: Putting these pieces together, we conclude that a noncitizen is "seeking admission" when he takes some kind of ongoing action to request lawful entry into the United States.

annotations.summary: Rejects the Sixth and Eleventh Circuit dissents: "deemed" in 1225(a)(1) creates a definition, as in TC Heartland, and even a legal fiction would not also deem applicants to be seeking admission.
annotations.quote: It is therefore best to understand § 1225(a)(1)'s use of the word "deemed" as creating a definition, not a legal fiction. Even if § 1225(a)(1) created a legal fiction, we are not so sure that legal fictions behave in the way our colleagues posit.

annotations.summary: Agrees "or otherwise" can signal a subset but holds it can also mean something different, as in Helsinn, so 1225(a)(3) does not compel the conclusion that all applicants are seeking admission.
annotations.quote: Without that disambiguation, § 1225(a)(3) does not compel the conclusion that all applicants for admission are necessarily seeking admission. Thus, § 1225(a)(3)'s "or otherwise" language does not turn the argument in the Government's favor.

annotations.summary: Holds the government's reading reads "seeking admission" out of the statute, violating the canon against surplusage and the presumption that different words carry different meanings; the government fails to show redundancy is more natural.
annotations.quote: However, these canons put a thumb on the scale in favor of giving "seeking admission" independent effect, and it is up to the Government to convince us that its redundant interpretation is the "more natural one."

annotations.summary: Reasons that 1226(c)'s exceptions for inadmissible people would be pointless under the government's reading, Preap makes 1226(c) a limit on 1226(a), and the Laken Riley Act ratified the border versus interior understanding.
annotations.quote: The Act therefore ratified the understanding and practice that § 1225(b)(2)(A) applies at the border while § 1226(a) applies to the interior.

annotations.summary: Relies on 1225's title, the 1996 practice of inspections at ports of entry, and the section's many references to arriving aliens to conclude that 1225(b)(2)(A) governs only the border.
annotations.quote: For starters, § 1225's title refers to "[i]nspection by immigration officers." When Congress enacted IIRIRA in 1996, immigration inspections took place at the border.

annotations.summary: Gives weight under Loper Bright and Learning Resources to nearly thirty years of executive practice across five administrations applying 1226 in the interior, beginning with the 1997 regulation.
annotations.quote: Over the course of the next five Presidential administrations, that understanding held. But in July 2025, the Government reversed course.

annotations.summary: Rejects the deeming argument partly because a single word in a definitional provision cannot hide an elephant in a mousehole by mandating bondless detention of millions.
annotations.quote: The word "deemed" cannot bear the weight of the millions of noncitizens it would potentially subject to detention without bond. For one, this construction would render the word "deemed" a mousehole hiding an elephant.

annotations.summary: Invokes constitutional avoidance as an additional reason: mandatory detention of millions without bond, unsupported by class wide findings like those in Demore, raises serious substantive due process concerns.
annotations.quote: The mandatory detention of potentially millions of noncitizens without the potential for bond raises exactly such serious concerns.

annotations.summary: Rejects the government's entry doctrine purpose argument: IIRIRA replaced only certain aspects of the old regime, Congress may have had reasons not to detain in the interior, and purpose cannot overcome text.
annotations.quote: While the Government's account is plausible, and many may agree with it as a matter of policy, it finds little purchase as an interpretive aid.

annotations.summary: Treats Jennings's description of 1225 at the border and 1226 in the interior as near binding dicta favoring the petitioner, and distinguishes Demore as resting on categorical congressional findings.
annotations.quote: In short, Jennings explained that § 1225 "authorizes the Government to detain certain aliens seeking admission into the country" while § 1226 "authorizes the Government to detain certain aliens already in the country."

annotations.summary: Holds that 1225(a)(1) gives "applicant for admission" a technical meaning, a passive condition of presence without admission, so its ordinary meaning cannot be used to equate it with seeking admission.
annotations.quote: we are required to look beyond ordinary meaning, because Congress has chosen to define the phrase "applicant for admission" in a technical and specific way.
cite: Hernandez Alvarez v. Warden, Fed. Det. Ctr. Miami

annotations.summary: Gives "seeking" its ordinary meaning of affirmative pursuit; the present participle signals an active, ongoing step toward lawful entry after inspection, which petitioners arrested after traffic stops were not taking.
annotations.quote: That the word is written as a present participle ("seeking") underscores that it is describing some active and temporally ongoing step or process on the part of the alien.
cite: Hernandez Alvarez v. Warden, Fed. Det. Ctr. Miami

annotations.summary: In a footnote, reads "deemed" as confirming a technical legal fiction, citing Sturgeon, that works precisely because the deemed class does not carry the ordinary meaning of applicant.
annotations.quote: This legal fiction functions not in spite of the term "applicant for admission" carrying its ordinary meaning, but precisely because it does not.
cite: Hernandez Alvarez v. Warden, Fed. Det. Ctr. Miami

annotations.summary: Calls 1225(a)(3) the government's strongest argument but holds "or otherwise" can denote something different, the structure is A or otherwise B or C or D, and Villarreal is distinguishable.
annotations.quote: At the outset, even if this reading of § 1225(a)(3) were correct, it would not contravene the plain text of § 1225(b)(2)(A).
cite: Hernandez Alvarez v. Warden, Fed. Det. Ctr. Miami

annotations.summary: Holds the government's reading makes "an alien seeking admission" surplusage; had Congress meant applicant status alone to trigger detention, it could have written the provision more simply.
annotations.quote: The Government's proffered reading also renders the phrase "an alien seeking admission" surplusage in the operation of § 1225(b)(2)(A), "an interpretative no-no."
cite: Hernandez Alvarez v. Warden, Fed. Det. Ctr. Miami

annotations.summary: Reasons that 1226(a) covers unadmitted people, 1226(c)'s inadmissibility exceptions and the Laken Riley Act's targeting of those who entered without inspection would be redundant under the government's reading.
annotations.quote: What's more, why would the Laken Riley Act target unadmitted aliens who were otherwise already included within the ambit of § 1225(b)(2)(A) by later adding a new and separate provision?
cite: Hernandez Alvarez v. Warden, Fed. Det. Ctr. Miami

annotations.summary: Reads 1225's titles and provisions as an inspection scheme for arriving aliens at the border, and holds seeking admission matters at examination by an officer, before removal proceedings begin.
annotations.quote: The INA's text confirms that the two relevant sections on detention govern distinct classes of aliens: § 1225 applies to arriving aliens seeking entry at the border, whereas § 1226 applies to aliens unlawfully in the interior.
cite: Hernandez Alvarez v. Warden, Fed. Det. Ctr. Miami

annotations.summary: Relies on the 1997 regulation and nearly thirty years of unbroken practice by five administrations, plus Congress leaving that construction untouched when it passed the Laken Riley Act.
annotations.quote: The original purpose in passing IIRIRA is confirmed by nearly thirty years of unbroken executive practice.
cite: Hernandez Alvarez v. Warden, Fed. Det. Ctr. Miami

annotations.summary: Notes Congress funded 500 beds and an escape hatch for 1226(c) yet made no capacity provision for the vast detention the government reads into 1225, suggesting no such mandate.
annotations.quote: No similar considerations were given for the sweeping detention provisions the Government says IIRIRA baked into § 1225. If Congress really had sought to launch such a detention campaign, it's a wonder Congress did not factor in the scale of new detentions when it was crunching the numbers
cite: Hernandez Alvarez v. Warden, Fed. Det. Ctr. Miami

annotations.summary: Applies skepticism toward sweeping claimed power and the elephants in mouseholes principle to reject reading 1225(a)(3) to mandate mass detention, while disclaiming reliance on the major questions doctrine itself.
annotations.quote: It produces a paradigmatic "elephant in a mousehole" that we are reluctant to embrace, hiding a sweeping reorientation of § 1225 inside an otherwise innocuous and separate provision that only addresses inspection.
cite: Hernandez Alvarez v. Warden, Fed. Det. Ctr. Miami

annotations.summary: Rejects the government's entry doctrine argument: legislative history shows IIRIRA modified only certain aspects, chiefly merging exclusion and deportation, with no sign Congress meant to overhaul detention.
annotations.quote: None of these important revisions, however, suggest Congress also sought to throw out the entry doctrine where federal detention authority was concerned.
cite: Hernandez Alvarez v. Warden, Fed. Det. Ctr. Miami

annotations.summary: Gives Jennings substantial weight as a detailed account of 1225 at the border and 1226 in the interior, and relies on Preap that 1226(c) limits 1226(a).
annotations.quote: We are obliged to afford Jennings some weight in how to view the provisions at issue today. Moreover, that the Court construed the INA in this manner in reaching its ultimate holding again suggests why our reading of the relevant provisions is most natural.
cite: Hernandez Alvarez v. Warden, Fed. Det. Ctr. Miami

annotations.summary: Argues 1225(a)(1) does not define "applicant for admission" with "means" but deems a class into it, so the phrase keeps its ordinary meaning, which the majority concedes matches seeking admission.
annotations.quote: That is not what Congress wrote. Section 1225(a)(1) does not "define" "applicant for admission" by listing its new meaning, set off by the word "means."
cite: Hernandez Alvarez v. Warden, Fed. Det. Ctr. Miami

annotations.summary: Argues an applicant necessarily seeks admission, and 1225(b)(2)(C)'s coverage of people arriving between ports shows "seeking admission" cannot require affirmative conduct toward inspected lawful entry.
annotations.quote: "Seeking admission" is not a description of what the alien is subjectively doing or intending. It is a consequence of what Congress has deemed him to be.
cite: Hernandez Alvarez v. Warden, Fed. Det. Ctr. Miami

annotations.summary: Relies on Sturgeon, Kaplan v. Tod, and Leng May Ma to argue a deeming clause carries the deemed category's consequences, so those deemed applicants are also seeking admission.
annotations.quote: If a person whom Congress has deemed an applicant for admission is not seeking admission, it is hard to know what Congress thought it was deeming him to be.
cite: Hernandez Alvarez v. Warden, Fed. Det. Ctr. Miami

annotations.summary: Relies on the en banc Villarreal rule that "or otherwise" is a catchall subsuming what precedes it, so 1225(a)(3) makes applicants for admission a subset of those seeking admission.
annotations.quote: "Applicants for admission" precedes "or otherwise." "Seeking admission" follows. Section 1225(a)(3) thus makes plain that applicants for admission are a subset of those seeking admission.
cite: Hernandez Alvarez v. Warden, Fed. Det. Ctr. Miami

annotations.summary: Calls the two phrases a doublet to which the surplusage canon does not apply, and argues the majority's reading creates worse surplusage by nullifying 1225(a)(1)'s coverage of present aliens.
annotations.quote: Doublet redundancy in a single sentence is a minor interpretive cost. Nullifying the reach of a deeming provision across an entire statutory section is not.
cite: Hernandez Alvarez v. Warden, Fed. Det. Ctr. Miami

annotations.summary: Argues 1226 keeps work under the government's reading, covering admitted people and deportable aliens, and that the Laken Riley Act closed a parole gap for criminal aliens rather than signaling 1226 coverage.
annotations.quote: It is unsurprising that, in the wake of the events that gave the Act its name, Congress wanted to foreclose "parole to aliens who have committed certain offenses."
cite: Hernandez Alvarez v. Warden, Fed. Det. Ctr. Miami

annotations.summary: Argues 1225(b)(2)(A) is not limited to border inspection: Congress expressly limited other 1225 provisions to arriving aliens, and the (b)(2) title covers "other aliens" like the petitioner.
annotations.quote: What is more, Congress demonstrated throughout § 1225 that it knew how to limit a provision to arriving aliens when it wished to do so.
cite: Hernandez Alvarez v. Warden, Fed. Det. Ctr. Miami

annotations.summary: Argues past practice is not clean: the 1997 rule said bond was available despite applicant status, 8 C.F.R. 235.3(b)(1)(ii) applied 1225(b)(2) to interior aliens, and unexercised authority does not evaporate.
annotations.quote: That the Executive long preferred flexibility over rigidity is not evidence that the mandatory authority was never conferred.
cite: Hernandez Alvarez v. Warden, Fed. Det. Ctr. Miami

annotations.summary: Responds that even the majority's reading mandates detention the government never had capacity for, and the statute's reach has never depended on the size of the population it covers.
annotations.quote: The statute's reach has never been constrained by the size of the population it describes.
cite: Hernandez Alvarez v. Warden, Fed. Det. Ctr. Miami

annotations.summary: Argues the major questions doctrine does not apply to a specific detention command in an area of overlapping political branch power, and that 1225(b)(2)(A) is no elephant in a mousehole.
annotations.quote: Regardless, Section 1225(b)(2)(A) does not present the kind of gap between statutory text and claimed executive power that the major questions doctrine polices.
cite: Hernandez Alvarez v. Warden, Fed. Det. Ctr. Miami

annotations.summary: Argues Jennings addressed prolonged detention, not this question; its framework description is dicta that also treated seeking entry and applicants for admission as interchangeable.
annotations.quote: If the majority wishes to accord Jennings's dicta special weight, it must take all of it, not just the portions it favors.
cite: Hernandez Alvarez v. Warden, Fed. Det. Ctr. Miami
